title: Booze News Weekly Roundup: U.S. Household Alcohol Spending Hits Record Low, EU Approves Chianti Rosé, and More
summary:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on household spending on alcohol in the U.S., the EU’s approval of Chianti rosé, the latest product releases, and more. content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on household spending on alcohol in the U.S., the EU’s approval of Chianti rosé, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Average U.S. household spending on alcohol hits record low: Alcohol purchases comprised a 0.77 percent share of the average U.S. household spending last year, a record low and 2 percent year-over-year drop, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Expenditure Survey. The average American household spent $630 on booze in 2025, down from $643 the previous year.
  • EU approves Chianti rosé distinction, other landmark amendments: Pink wine will now be a recognized category in Chianti, Tuscany’s largest and most popular wine sub-region. The European Union approved the distinction as part of a total overhaul of Chianti’s wine production regulations, which also lowered the minimum amount of Sangiovese to be considered a Chianti blend.
  • National Wine and Spirits (NWS) challenges $6.6 million payment to RNDC’s parent company: NWS filed a complaint against RNDC last week to prevent it from paying $6.57 million to its parent company. NWS and RNDC were previously in a joint venture for Kentucky’s liquor distribution business before selling it to KEG 1 Kentucky after RNDC’s fallout. As part of the plan, a portion of the money from that sale, roughly $6.6 million, was set to go to RNDC’s parent company to offset debts. NWS is arguing that RDNC damaged the joint venture and that NWS is entitled to a portion of the buyout.
  • Sazerac’s bullish shopping spree shows no signs of slowing: The Louisville, Ky.-based spirits juggernaut bought Oregon craft brewery Full Sail Brewing for an undisclosed sum and launched a $605 million project to expand four of its Kentucky distilleries. These advancements come in the same year as Sazerac’s pickups of ready-to-drink brands Dirty Shirley and Au Vodka, as well as its $15 billion attempt at scooping Brown-Forman.
  • DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart for $17 billion: The landmark deal, announced last Thursday, will loop the U.S.’s largest grocery delivery app under the same umbrella as the country’s biggest takeout service. The transaction values Instacart shares at $65 each.

Product releases to watch:

  • The Macallan releases the final iteration of special New Years Eve series: The Macallan is closing out A Night on Earth, an annual series geared toward celebrating different cultures’ New Years Eve celebrations, with a limited-edition single malt. The Finale, the collection’s fifth installment, honors New Orleans and is available online and at The Macallan Estate Boutique for a suggested retail price of $125.
  • WhistlePig gets indulgent with dessert-like rye: WhistlePig is debuting 12-Year Single Finish Maple Crème Brûlée Rye, a whiskey inspired by wintry, holiday flavors. The limited-edition rye aged in the brand’s ex-maple syrup barrels, which were charred to mimic the burnt sugar flavors of crème brûlée. WhistlePig’s Maple Crème Brûlée is now available online and at select retailers, bars, and restaurants for a suggested price of $124.99.
  • Tears of Llorona debuts a five-year-old extra añejo: The premium Jalisco tequila brand is releasing its latest small-batch extra añejo later this month. Hills of Los Altos aged for five years — two years over the minimum — and will be available in limited quantities for a suggested retail price of $279.99.

title: People Have Been Ranking Cheap Beers For Decades. The Appeal Lives On.
summary:
I recently somehow added Google Discover to my iPhone and suddenly I was getting push notifications for content it thought I might like to read. It was annoying at first, but I had to admit the picks were usually spot-on with my interests. Hosannas to Michael Olise’s latest stunning performance in the Champions League. Critical reviews of “You Can See Everything.” Reviews for the new Georgian restaurant in my neighborhood.

The article People Have Been Ranking Cheap Beers For Decades. The Appeal Lives On. appeared first on VinePair.
content:
I recently somehow added Google Discover to my iPhone and suddenly I was getting push notifications for content it thought I might like to read. It was annoying at first, but I had to admit the picks were usually spot-on with my interests.

Hosannas to Michael Olise’s latest stunning performance in the Champions League.

Critical reviews of “You Can See Everything.”

Reviews for the new Georgian restaurant in my neighborhood.

And one morning a few weeks ago, I got pushed a just-published Tasting Table story entitled: I Tried 11 Cheap Beers And Ranked Them Worst To Best

I didn’t need to know who wrote it. I didn’t even need to read it yet. I knew it would be a viral hit.

Indeed, within days the article would be widely shared on social media and message boards and syndicated by Yahoo Life and AOL. (For what it’s worth, author Julia Duda would select Miller High Life for “its impeccable balance between crispness and flavor.”)

Now entering its fourth decade of existence, the “cheap beers ranked” listicle is seemingly, still, one of the most reliable ways for a publication to garner easy viral traffic.

Consuming Reports

June 1996. Consumer Reports, that ad-free arbiter of car, appliance, and electronics quality, decided to, for the first time, put its powers of evaluation toward “mass-marketed beers.” They gathered 17 academically-trained beer tasters (brewmasters and PhDs in fermentation sciences mainly) to determine the “blue-collar bargain of the beer cooler” by tasting 69 different beers.

The winner was Old Milwaukee, then the second cheapest beer in the country, averaging $1.69 per 6-pack. Second place was even more surprising — Stroh’s, created by German immigrants in 1850, and not even a top 25 best-selling beer in America by 1996. Third place got even stranger, being awarded to Red Dog, a now-defunct product from Miller.

Even in this mid-1990s nascent era of craft beer and online chatter, the unexpected results went viral — print viral.

The Washington Post covered it, quite aghast at the report and with a ton of editorializing from writer Marc Fisher. “[The result] makes sense — if the Old Milwaukee had been delivered to the tasters by Learjet, while competitors’ brews were placed in blinding sunlight for several years.”

The article was covered by The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, and Tampa Bay Times. AP business writer Brian S. Akre asked “Could it be that Bud’s been dethroned as the King of Beers?” While the New York Daily News thought “Magazine Ratings are Hard to Swallow” and gathered 25 of their own employees to conduct their own tasting.

Though surely earnest in their intentions, Consumer Reports had unwittingly taught the mainstream media that rating cheap beers could inspire such intense debate that virality was all but guaranteed. The race was on, and for the next 30 years “cheap beers ranked” has been as dependable an article as one can publish.

The Best Worst

These listicles would mostly remain the purview of print for the first decade of the 21st century. The Washington Post would do their own cheap beer blind taste test in 2009, defining that as ones priced at less than $6 a sixer. Baltimore’s beloved local lager National Bohemian would win and the story would be covered by NPR and others.

It would take modern internet culture — and the rise of high-priced craft beer — however, to launch “cheap beers ranked” into the stratosphere. Audiences have all but demanded this story.

In 2012, Slate offered its readers a chance to assign a feature to one of its authors. The top seven picks — which included “Make Seth Stevenson explain the scourge of scaffolding” and “Make Matt Yglesias explain why hotel rooms cost so much” — were voted on, and ultimately the winner was “Make Troy Patterson review cheap beers.”

His resulting article, “The Best Worst Brews,” didn’t really rank beers but just had him trying and offering his thoughts on some cheap notables like Natural Light (“If you’re having only one beer, Natty Light is one to avoid.”). Perhaps due to his wishy-washy thoughts and lack of a forced ranking, the story only received one comment and, so far as I can tell, is just about the only cheap beers ranked listicle to not go viral. Maybe Slate should have opted for that Yglesias story.

In 2013, just as craft beer was undergoing a massive boom and clearly differentiating itself from the macros, offbeat sports blog Deadspin, then at the peak of its powers, offered “36 Cheap American Beers, Ranked.”

Author Will Gordon would stir debate by blasting beloved favorites like Miller High Life and Yuengling while crowning Minnesota’s Grain Belt Premium as his No. 1. As I’ve written about before, this was an era where you could go insanely viral on the internet and this piece did massive numbers, with over 2 million views, thousands of comments on the article itself, and a colossal amount of sharing it across the World Wide Web. Gordon appeared on AM radio and podcasts to discuss it and CBS News even did a report on it.

It ended up being Deadspin’s 7th most popular post of the year — in a year they uncovered the Manti Te’o dead girlfriend hoax — and might very well be the most widely-read piece of beer criticism ever written.

So seismic was Gordon’s article that other websites tried to quickly draft off the traffic, like First We Feast, which posted “America’s Best Cheap Beers, Ranked” a mere day later, even addressing its inspiration.

“Yesterday, writer Will Gordon set a certain segment of the suds-swilling, butt-scratching Internet on fire,” wrote then-editor-in-chief of First We Feast (and future “Hot Ones” creator) Chris Schonberger. “Since we’d been working on our own cheap-beer rankings in honor of July 4, our first thought was, ‘Damn, we’ve been scooped!’, followed shortly by, Oh wait, this is not an original idea at all!’, and then finally — upon reading through Gordon’s hastily summarized picks — ‘This list completely blows!’”

Schonberger would end up ranking Narragansett Lager as his No. 1, which incidentally Gordon had already ranked as his No. 2.

I think Gordon’s article was such a hit because he went above and beyond everyone else who had ever done it before, ranking 36 different beers, including plenty of beloved local lagers like Iron City, Olympia, Rainier, and Lone Star, while not being afraid to take down sacred cows. There was something for literally everyone to applaud — or be pissed off about — in an era where Twitter was likewise at its zenith and everybody had something to say and post.

Even Gordon, who would offer rebuttal to himself the very next year when he published for Deadspin a mea culpa that “Schlitz Is America’s Best Cheap Beer.” He had previously ranked it No. 30.

From Awful to Drinkable

You would think that would be the end of it, but no, the cheap beers listicle would storm on into the second half of the decade.

The Washington Post yet again went to the well in 2016, keying in on canned beers sold in D.C. bars for $4 or less. New York’s Genesee Cream Ale would prevail. A website called Cheapism would do their own rankings in 2016, considering anything $10 or less per 6-pack.

And, yes, of course, we here at VinePair have done it too, with two separate cheap beer lists penned in 2017 alone. There was “8 Cheap Light Beers, Ranked” (the little discussed Bud Light Platinum won), and the “11 Cheap American Beers Ranked From Awful to Drinkable” (or Natural Ice to Narragansett) which reeled in a cool 1.2 million views.

Over the last decade, cheap beers have been ranked by Maxim, Gear Patrol, Uproxx, Delish, Paste, Outside, Taste of Home, Wide Open Country, The Takeout, and Porch Drinking.

We haven’t even discussed the countless free alt-weeklies, college newspapers, personal blogs, message boards, and YouTube videos (8 million views!) offering their own rankings.

And here we are in 2026, an era where the cheap beers listicle improbably still prevails. Things have changed, though, and the lists have likewise changed with the times.

If those initial lists two and three decades ago mostly only included multinational-owned American adjunct lagers, slowly but surely cheap Mexican lagers started appearing as well — matching the rise of the category itself — as did so-called “supermarket craft beers” like Brooklyn Lager, which took the top spot when Food & Wine published We Ranked 20 Mass-Market North American Lagers by Taste Alone — Here’s Who Won just this June. (For what it’s worth, Brooklyn Lager was actually one of the more expensive pints one could buy when I first moved to New York in 2000.)

More importantly, and perhaps as the authors of these articles have shifted from jaded Gen X writers to Millennials and now Zoomers, the idea of these lists as ironic counterpoints to the rise of craft beer has begun to fade and most publications are now publishing these listicles more earnestly. Like Chowhound, who in July offered Ranking Cheap Beer Brands From The Least Drinkable To The Absolute Best. Author Sarah Dealy noted that these beers are “near and dear to my heart,” even going on to explain that she’s never been a fan of expensive double IPAs that cost $9 a pint. She, like Duda at Tasting Table, opted for Miller High Life as her No. 1.

Cheap Cheep

Beer, like life, is only getting more expensive.

People are losing interest in craft beer and that old “macro vs. craft” war is all but over.

But everyone still has their own opinion on and, theoretically, can afford cheap beer. Perhaps that’s why once-maligned, low-brow brands like Busch Light are all of a sudden booming in sales. People can’t afford to be snarky toward swill any more. Likewise, a cheap beer listicle might be the least expensive piece of tasting content a food or drink publication can produce.

It’s easy to tell a just-out-of-college freelancer to go review 10 macro beers — they’ll have already tasted most and already formed an opinion on plenty. It would be harder to get them to assess the best papalote mezcals on the market. And, as the spirits editor here, I’m sad to admit that also would get a lot less traffic as I doubt most people have had or have strong thoughts on, say, the Sanzekan Papalote ‘Eufemio Sanchez.’

The cheap beer listicle is an idea that has outlived print, personal blogs, message board culture, Twitter, and Deadspin (now owned by a digital media company in Malta!), and is now basically the last evergreen feature that will surely outlive us all. The next incarnation of these lists will probably be written by AI agents, but it doesn’t take a supercomputer to know how to reel readers in. You just need the headline.

In fact, just yesterday as I write this, Google Discover pushed me yet another story entitled “The Hands-Down Best Cheap Beer Isn’t Pabst Blue Ribbon or Miller Lite.”

I couldn’t help myself. I clicked.

title: 15 Popular Regional Bar Snacks From Around the World, Mapped
summary:
The tradition of snacking on something salty, cheesy, or nutty while imbibing at a local bar can be traced back centuries. And still today, drinkers just can’t resist having a bowl of peanuts or potato chips to accompany a crisp pint of beer after a work day or a dish of olives with an afternoon spritz. But beyond these classic small bites, each corner of the world has developed a certain set of bar snacks that go along with its particular drinking culture.

The article 15 Popular Regional Bar Snacks From Around the World, Mapped appeared first on VinePair.
content:
The tradition of snacking on something salty, cheesy, or nutty while imbibing at a local bar can be traced back centuries. And still today, drinkers just can’t resist having a bowl of peanuts or potato chips to accompany a crisp pint of beer after a work day or a dish of olives with an afternoon spritz. But beyond these classic small bites, each corner of the world has developed a certain set of bar snacks that go along with its particular drinking culture. For some countries this means bites of cheese-filled fritters between sips of a local brew, while others lean lighter with easygoing seafood dishes to complement bright, crisp wines.

These distinct snacks can be seen at watering holes across the globe, and in some places, like New York City, you can experience a world of bar snacks in one afternoon: from the spice bag at Bar Snack in the East Village to the pork scratchings at the West Village’s own British pub, Dean’s. While New Yorkers are lucky to have easy access to just about any world cuisine at establishments around the city, these bar snacks have interesting origin stories of their own.

No matter what you snack on when knocking back a cold one, it’s important — if not enriching — to understand the cultural ties of those dishes. From the spice-laced peanuts of Mexico and China to deep-fried balls of meat from Western Europe, here are the most popular bar snacks around the world.

Europe

Italy

Stuzzichini

You can almost always expect small ramekins of salty and appetite-whetting snacks to arrive alongside each round of Aperol Spritzes, Negronis, Garibaldis, and the like on cocktail-hour tables across Italy. The northwest city of Turin was the birthplace of the tradition of the Italian aperitivo hour, where the 18th-century advent of vermouth sparked a ritual of pre-dinner, low-ABV drinks and small bites. Stuzzichini are the small, usually savory snacks served during aperitivo hour. The customary mix of small dishes might include taralli — ring-shaped, baked crackers that either come plain or flavored with herbs — olives, peanuts, or even potato chips.

United Kingdom

Scotch Eggs

Coming from the U.K. — where pub culture involves hefty beers and hearty snacks to match — is the Scotch egg. The dish is a hard- or soft-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, coated in breadcrumbs, and fried. While its name suggests it originated in Scotland, most food historians believe English cooks first invented the Scotch egg in the 18th century. (One retail store in London claims to have been among the first to make the dish in 1738). Some accounts also theorize that Scotch eggs emerged as a result of the transfer of cultures between the U.K. and India via the East India Company. Those claims say Scotch eggs were a British take on Nargisi Kofta, a traditional Indian dish of a similar format, with a cooked egg encased in spiced ground meat.

Pork Scratchings

Pork scratchings are slices of pig skin that are dehydrated and fried until they puff into an airy, crackingly crisp texture. Already rich in meaty and umami flavors, pork scratchings are often seasoned with just a dash of salt. What differentiates scratchings from “rinds” or “cracklings” is that they usually come from the skin on the pig’s hind legs. Similar to Scotch eggs, the rich, deep-fried flavor of pork scratchings serves to complement the heavy profile of pub-style brews. They first came about among impoverished communities in 1800s England, where people used every last bit of the livestock for a cheap, filling snack. Today, pork snatchings are often sold in retail stores packaged in bags or served fresh at pubs.

Germany

Pretzels

No, German pretzels aren’t just an Instagrammable fad for tourists to pose with while in their lederhosen at Munich’s biergartens. The snack dates back to the Middle Ages, and some historians think an Italian monk was the first to tie a simple dough into a knot as a symbol of the Christian Holy Trinity. In the 1100s, the tradition then spread to what is now Germany, when the famous shape of the knotted bread became the go-to signage for bakeries. Today, the salted snack is served at bars around the world. In Germany, pretzels are most often soft and can be an accompaniment to beers served in mugs or steins.

Spain

Gildas

Gildas come from Spain’s Basque Country — the stretch of land between northeast Spain and southwest France, where the cuisine is centered around seafood and small bites. The handheld snack is presented on a small skewer, with bites alternating between green olives, pickled hot peppers, and anchovies cured in oil. While now ubiquitous around Spain and at Basque-inspired restaurants around the world, Gildas didn’t come about until the 20th century: San Sebastián’s Bar Casa Vallés first introduced the dish in 1946 after a regular customer skewered the three ingredients together and consumed the ensemble as one. Some snackers like to take each element individually, whereas others eat them in the same bite. No matter how you go at it, gildas bring strong, piquant flavors of brine, vinegar, and spice and commonly accompany a glass of Txakoli or vermouth — two popular choices at Spanish bars.

Croquetas

Croquetas are now most common at Spanish tapas bars and restaurants, but the French were the first to shape leftover meat scraps — and eventually béchamel — into a ball to then bread and fry them. But it wasn’t until the Spanish adopted the dish in the 1800s that it became as popular around the world as it is today. On tapas menus, croquetas take many different forms. Most traditional are the croquetas de jamón, but bargoers can also find examples with chicken, cod, or cheese.. Croquetas are particularly popular in Catalonia, where light, sessionable beers like Estrella Damm or bottles of bubbly Cava are common for washing down the heavy snack.

Ireland

Spice Bag

Consumed as both late-night street food and a pub snack alongside a Guinness, spice bags are one of Ireland’s latest claims to fame. While the name doesn’t reveal much about what’s inside, it refers to a mixture of crispy fried chicken, french fries, peppers, and onions all haphazardly thrown into a bag, doused in dry spices, and shaken together. At its core, spice bags are a blend of Irish pub food and Chinese flavors: Most accounts say Sunflower Chinese, a takeout spot in Dublin, invented the now-popular snack in 2006. Some may say spice bags are best when eaten after a few pints to satiate your appetite, but the balance of a spicy kick with the toasted, chocolatey notes of Guinness is some great craic.

The Netherlands

Bitterballen

Similar to croquetas, bitterballen are deep fried orbs with a crisp, craggly breadcrumb exterior that gives way to a creamy, meaty filling. Traditional recipes combine a roux with chunks of cooked meat — usually beef — and its juices to create an incredibly rich, velvety mouthfeel. While their exact origin is unknown, bitterballen are believed to have emerged during the 1600s. Now common at traditional bars in Amsterdam and across the Netherlands, the snack is usually dipped in a bright, spicy mustard to cut through the unctuous flavors. Bitterballan also accompany crisp Dutch lagers like Amstel or Heineken.

North America

United States

Chicken Wings

Whether at a dive, sports, or a regular neighborhood bar in the U.S., you can bet chicken wings will be on the menu. The spicy, bright orange Buffalo sauce may be the most common to dress chicken wings, but with the Buffalo wing’s ubiquity came the expansion of options, with lemon-pepper, barbecue, and garlic-parmesan sauces now popular on menus. On the side usually comes a ramekin of ranch or bleu cheese dressing and spears of celery and carrots to cut through the spicy, salty, and fatty elements. Chicken wings became so beloved within the American consumer consciousness that national and international chains like Buffalo Wild Wings and Wing Stop have become a go-to. Chicken wings are often relegated to more laid-back establishments like dives or sports bars and often consumed with light beers — though, they arguably go with anything.

Nachos

Nachos originated in Mexico, not far from the Texas border. And while the dish — a heaping pile of tortilla chips most commonly covered in toppings like queso, beans, meat, and jalapeños — is still popular in its home country, the U.S. has taken it in as its own. Relatively easy to execute and share among a table of people, nachos are the ultimate communal dish to enjoy alongside a few Margaritas.

Mexico

Cacahuates Botaneros

Originating from the southern Mexico region of Oaxaca, “cacahuates botaneros” roughly translates to “bar snack peanuts.” You can find the snack at the center of a table of cervezas, micheladas, Margaritas, or Palomas. The dish traditionally mixes peanuts with a number of seasonings, such as garlic, chilis, oil, salt, and lime juice, before toasting the ensemble over a stove. A halved lime usually comes beside a bowl of the nuts to brighten everything up.

Asia

Korea

Corn Cheese

Corn cheese, known locally as kon-chijeu, is a Korean dip that’s exactly as it sounds: a warm mix of corn and melted cheese. A combination of the corn, mozzarella, mayonnaise, and other ingredients is baked in a skillet and, immediately after removing from the oven, topped with slices of scallions or chives and served sizzling hot. It first gained popularity around the late 20th century, but it is now a common food to snack on while drinking in South Korea. Corn cheese is one of the many dishes in the “anju” category — a suite of modern Korean drinking snacks that also includes fried chicken, shredded squid, and blood sausage.

China

Drunken Peanuts

Coming from the Szechuan region in China — an area beloved for a cuisine that often features a numbing peppercorn spice — drunken peanuts (also known as jiǔguǐ huāshēng) got their name from being a popular snack at bars, where they are usually consumed with beer. The peanuts are either fried or roasted before getting the mala seasoning treatment, which is a blend of red chili peppers and Szechuan peppercorns. There’s little account of drunken peanuts’ origins other than their long ties to Szechuan cuisine, but in recent years, the snack has commercialized, with a number of companies packaging the peanuts to be sold in retail stores.

Japan

Chicken Karaage

A popular dish at Japanese izakaya bars, chicken Karaage is a crispy, crunchy snack of fried chicken to enjoy with an ice cold Asahi or crisp Toki highball. It’s made by frying up small pieces of thigh meat marinated in a ginger, soy sauce, and garlic dressing. The dish actually has origins in China, where deep frying bite-sized foods was first common and then brought to Japan. It especially spread around Japan after World War II, when food became sparse and frying pieces of chicken became a cheap alternative for a satiating meal.

South America

Brazil

Coxinha

Coxinhas are fried, cone-shaped bites filled with chicken with spices, onions, garlic, and cheese. There are a number of theories about the origins of the dish — some involve Brazilian royalty, and others say it was a natural extension of French croquettes. The word “coxhina” translates to “little thigh” in Portuguese, which some say is a nod to the fried dish’s teardrop-like appearance that is made to resemble the drumstick of a chicken. Both a street food and a bar snack, coxinhas are served with light, easy-drinking beers.

*Image retrieved from WS Studio via unsplash.com

title: We Asked 16 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Underrated Pinot Noir?
summary:
Though it has centuries of history in Burgundy, great quality Pinot Noir can now be found in every corner of the world, from the volcanic Otago peninsula in New Zealand to the high plateaus of Greece’s Amyndeon region. Across these different areas, Pinot Noir offers a wide variety of expressions, from dense, fruit-forward examples full of juicy cherry and strawberry notes to delicate versions with subtle hints of earth and spice. The number of Pinot Noir styles available across a world of winegrowing regions can be overwhelming, and often results in sticking to your default pick at the store.

The article We Asked 16 Sommeliers: What’s the Most Underrated Pinot Noir? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Though it has centuries of history in Burgundy, great quality Pinot Noir can now be found in every corner of the world, from the volcanic Otago peninsula in New Zealand to the high plateaus of Greece’s Amyndeon region. Across these different areas, Pinot Noir offers a wide variety of expressions, from dense, fruit-forward examples full of juicy cherry and strawberry notes to delicate versions with subtle hints of earth and spice.

The number of Pinot Noir styles available across a world of winegrowing regions can be overwhelming, and often results in sticking to your default pick at the store. But exploring underappreciated producers and regions can yield delightful results — and often at a cheaper price point. To discover which wines deserve more time in the spotlight, we asked 16 sommeliers to name the most underrated Pinot Noir on the market right now. From up-and-coming German Spätburgunders to fresh, coastal Californian wines, here’s what they said.

The most underrated Pinot Noir, according to sommeliers:

  • Redbank Pinot Noir 2021
  • German Pinot Noir
  • Sante Arcangeli Split Rail Vineyard Pinot Noir
  • San Luis Obispo Coast Pinot Noir
  • Belle Pente Willamette Valley Pinot Noir
  • Greek Pinot Noir
  • The Ojai Vineyard ‘Fe Ciega Discípulo’ Pinot Noir 2021
  • Japanese Pinot Noir
  • Argentinian Pinot Noir
  • Niedrist Pinot Nero Riserva 2020
  • By Farr ‘Farrside’ Pinot Noir
  • New Zealand Pinot Noir
  • Domaine Vincent Dureuil-Janthial Coteaux Bourguignons
  • Domaine Michel Magnien Coteaux Bourguignons
  • Marine Layer ‘Lyra’ Pinot Noir
  • Walker Bay Pinot Noir

“For me, the most underrated Pinot Noir is the 2021 Redbank Pinot Noir from King Valley, Australia. I was fortunate enough to find this randomly, and it blew my mind. Light, fresh, and irresistible, it’s out the door for $20 at my shop, and people LOVE it!” —Thomas Price, beverage director, 1856 – Culinary Residence, Auburn, Ala.

“German Pinot Noir! The wine coming out of Baden especially has had the majority of sommeliers’ attention for years, and the general public is slowly catching on as well. Herbal and light in body, but deeply complex — they’re wines for enjoyment as well as contemplation. I predict that these wines will only get better as the region’s producers’ experience grows and climate change takes more effect. Wasenhaus and Enderle & Moll are my favorite Pinot Noir producers in Germany, but if you can get your hands on a bottle of Wasenhaus’ single vineyard Möhlin, you’re in for a real treat.” —Christian DiNello, wine director, Indienne and Elder, New York City

“The Santa Cruz Mountains don’t get the recognition they deserve, and the Sante Arcangeli Split Rail Vineyard Pinot Noir is a beautiful example of why they should. Grown at 1,700 feet, it offers expressive aromas of pine, redwood forest, and freshly sanded cedar that keep drawing your nose back to the glass. Light on its feet and wonderfully elegant, it reveals a spicy cranberry, red cherry, and blackberry fruit profile.” —Lance Tolaio, beverage director, Sam’s Grill, San Francisco

“Pinot Noir from the San Luis Obispo Coast is some of the most exciting, fresh examples of Pinot Noir that I’ve experienced recently. With voices like Lady of the Sunshine, Scar of the Sea, and Phelan Farm, among others, there is no shortage of dedicated winemakers who are also very connected to the vineyards; often, they are the ones farming. The sites are a stone’s throw from the bay, giving the Pinot Noirs a unique lift and vibrancy, a slight umami edge with delicate red berry, and spice unique to this special place.” —Kim Prokoshyn, sommelier and general manager, Dunn & Sons Wine, Yarmouth Port, Mass.

“At Lansdowne in Portland, Ore., We proudly celebrate Pacific Northwest wines exclusively, and Pinot Noir is king! With its bright acidity, silky-smooth tannins, and expressive red-fruit flavors, we love how Pinot Noir from our own ‘neighborhood’ can be youthful and approachable while still offering elegance, depth, and complexity — making it the perfect partner for our thoughtful, seasonal menu. My absolute favorite Willamette Valley Pinot Noir comes from Belle Pente, whose wines beautifully capture the soul of the valley and a true sense of place!” —Owen Perry, wine director, Lansdowne, Portland, Ore.

“When we think of Pinot Noir, Greece is probably not the first country that comes to mind, and that is exactly why it deserves a closer look. From northern Greece to the Peloponnese, diverse climates, elevations, and soils offer intriguing possibilities for this delicate variety; producers such as Papaioannou, Moschopolis, and Alpha Estate are worth discovering. Greek Pinot Noir remains an under-the-radar discovery for wine lovers willing to look beyond the usual suspects.” —Despoina Karapostolaki, sommelier, Delos Greek Restaurant, NYC

“The greatest source of underappreciated Pinot Noir may be the German region of Baden. Bernhard Huber, now helmed by his son Julian, is an incredible producer crafting Burgundy-level quality in his home region of Malterdingen. The wines are always ripe, textured, and elegant. The cooler climate helps keep alcohol levels lower, resulting in brilliantly drinkable Pinot!” —Ryan McGuinness, assistant manager and beverage director, Shipwright’s Daughter, Mystic, Conn.

“I recommend Ojai Vineyard Fe Ciega ‘Discípulo’ Pinot Noir from Sta. Rita Hills, California. This wine hovers under the radar. It’s not flashy, rich, fruity, or sweetly luscious; it’s earthy, iron-driven, and floral, with notes of amaro and an inviting structure. Maybe it’s because of its locality, or maybe the name is too tricky to pronounce.” —Mandy Monzyk, wine director, Miller & Lux, San Francisco

“Japan is still overlooked as a source of Pinot Noir in the U.S., and Coco Farm’s 2021 Pinot Noir deserves more attention. Coco Farm is based in Ashikaga, Tochigi, but this wine is made in Hokkaido using grapes grown in Yoichi. The unusually hot, dry 2021 growing season gave it rich, ripe berry flavors, aromas of spice and smoked meat, and a smooth, full-bodied texture. At Soba Ulala, I love it with our Wagyu or beef soba, as the generous fruit complements the richness of the beef and the sweet and savory flavors of the broth.” —Hirohisa Hayashi, owner, chef, and sommelier, Soba Ulala, NYC

“These days I’m super into Pinot Noir from Germany. The country seems to be benefiting from the climate changes happening across the world. Whereas I used to think German Pinot was a bit tart (too cool of a climate for it), now it is spot on for it and thriving! Some producers to watch for are Leipold and Enderle & Moll. And another area I am loving is Altamira in Mendoza. It is the highest elevation region in Mendoza, and it also benefits from being right at the heel of the Andes mountains that divide Argentina with Chile. Chalk and limestone soils and a cool climate make for really incredible Pinot. Finca Suarez, a seventh generation winemaker, is starting to export its Pinot Noir, and another favorite of mine is the Canopus project.” —Tamy Rofe, wine director and co-owner, Colonia Verde and Ibérico, Brooklyn

“The world’s fascination with Pinot Noir often overlooks hidden gems high in the alpine valleys of Alto Adige. The Niedrist Pinot Nero Riserva 2020 is an elegant expression of Pinot Noir from Alto Adige, where alpine influences, dramatic diurnal temperature shifts, and mineral-rich soils create wines of remarkable finesse and precision. Produced by the esteemed Niedrist family in the hills surrounding Cornaiano, the wine reflects the estate’s commitment to meticulous vineyard management and restrained winemaking. The 2020 vintage offers expressive aromas of wild cherry, raspberry, rose petal, and subtle baking spice, complemented by earthy undertones and finely integrated oak. Silky tannins, vibrant acidity, and a lingering mineral finish give this wine a beautiful balance of Burgundian elegance and distinctive Alpine character.” —Jason Alexander, wine director, Back Home Hospitality, San Francisco

“By Farr’s ‘Farrside’ Pinot Noir remains one of the most overlooked values in fine wine, offering a level of complexity, structure, and terroir expression that would command a considerably higher price in Burgundy. Grown in the cool climate of Geelong, Farrside combines depth and concentration with the elegance, savory complexity, and mineral tension often associated with Burgundy’s finest premier cru vineyards. The Farr family brings decades of experience in the vineyard and cellar, with a winemaking philosophy shaped by their work in both Australia and Burgundy and a deep understanding of the land they farm. Farrside is a compelling example of what Australian Pinot Noir can achieve, offering the character, pedigree, and age-worthiness of serious Burgundy without the price that so often accompanies its reputation.” —Christian Shaum, sommelier, Asador Bastian, Chicago

“I want to mention New Zealand Pinot Noir, which often punches well above its price point, effortlessly combining New World fruit generosity with Old World elegance, earthiness, and complexity. There’s impressive diversity, too, from the bold, concentrated wines of Central Otago to the savory, structured Pinots of Martinborough and the fragrant expressions of Marlborough, with a strong commitment to sustainable viticulture across the country. And please don’t judge a wine by its screw cap; New Zealand puts some seriously spectacular Pinot Noir under these closures, proving that great wine doesn’t need a cork to have class!” —Ola Rybka, sommelier, TIYA, San Francisco

“In an age where the great Pinot Noirs of Burgundy are becoming increasingly more expensive, I find myself still wanting a great glass of Burgundy with my roasted chicken on a Wednesday evening. The wines of Coteaux Bourguignons have been my solution to this conundrum as of late. Created under its current name in November 2011, it covers a large geographic area where winemakers are legally allowed to source fruit, and many of the top producers in Burgundy have used this to their advantage to produce a more affordable entry into their portfolios. Do your research before purchasing, because this appellation also allows Gamay and it is often blended with Pinot Noir in this AOC. Two of my favorites are from Vincent Dureuil-Janthial and Michel Magnien, they provide incredible value and overdeliver for the price of every vintage.” —John Leight, sommelier, Salamander Middleburg, Middleburg, Va.

“As a California restaurant uplifting local and sustainable producers, we are truly privileged to feature Marine Layer’s ‘Lyra’ Pinot Noir at Tomat. This wine has been on our by-the-glass menu for many moons, and continues to be a revelation to our guests. The production methods are as impressive as the end product — the fruit is picked by hand at night from select Sonoma sites that celebrate a variety of microclimates and Pinot Noir clones, fermented with 35 percent whole clusters, and then barrel aged for 11 months. With vibrant red berry fruit, spice, and crushed flowers laced with a kiss of French oak, it is not only deftly crafted, but goes exceptionally well with food. From salads and crudo to duck, pork, and beef, this wine is a California stunner.” —Natalie Dial, co-owner and wine director, Tomat, Los Angeles

“The most underrated Pinot Noir is from South Africa, particularly from Walker Bay. The wines are just really well made and offer good value for their quality. Guests have always been pleasantly surprised every time they try a Pinot Noir from South Africa.” —Justin Chin, general manager and sommelier, The Happy Crane, San Francisco

Follow Farmer’s Gin at @farmersgin or visit farmersgin.com.

Bateman’s is one of New York’s “if you know, you know” bars. While other East Village cocktail spots have opened to plenty of fanfare, owners Natasha Van Duser and Carlo Olcese took a quieter approach to building Bateman’s into one of the city’s great bars. Rather than compete for the spotlight, they used the neighborhood’s booming cocktail scene to their advantage, initially drawing in curious drinkers as they moved between East Village hottest spots.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Natasha joins Adam to discuss how COVID brought about the idea for Bateman’s, why opening in the East Village was so important, and what inspired them to create a bar set inside the world of American Psycho.

title: At Portland’s Papi, a Pornstar Martini Riff Is Topped with Cava Custard Foam
summary:
It’s no secret that foam is among the most popular drink garnishes of today. From cloud-topped coffees and side-pulled beer pours to frozen cocktails with dollops of salted mascarpone, frothy drinks are popping up in just about every corner of the beverage sector. Bartenders, baristas, and consumers alike just can’t get enough of the thick, creamy topping — whether it be for the trend’s undeniable visual appeal or the unique textural experience that the first sip delivers.

The article At Portland’s Papi, a Pornstar Martini Riff Is Topped with Cava Custard Foam appeared first on VinePair.
content:
It’s no secret that foam is among the most popular drink garnishes of today. From cloud-topped coffees and side-pulled beer pours to frozen cocktails with dollops of salted mascarpone, frothy drinks are popping up in just about every corner of the beverage sector. Bartenders, baristas, and consumers alike just can’t get enough of the thick, creamy topping — whether it be for the trend’s undeniable visual appeal or the unique textural experience that the first sip delivers.

As these towering garnishes reach new heights and populate more menus, bartenders are tasked with finding innovative ways to put their own spin on the technique. Izzy Stein, beverage and creative director at Papi in Portland, Maine, felt compelled to take the aerated trend in her own direction. The result is the Mami Chula, a tall, bright orange cocktail flecked with passion fruit seeds and vanilla bean, topped, of course, with a stunning cupcake-icing-like swirl of Cava custard foam.

When designing the Mami Chula, Stein started with the concept of the foam before finding the right drink for it to sit atop. She first crafted the creamy Cava-custard mixture while trying to develop a crème brûlée-inspired Pisco Sour. Instead, she eventually landed on a Pornstar Martini-esque drink. “It was a little bit of a scavenger hunt, starting from a small concept and then just building around that,” she says.

To make the foam, Stein begins by reducing a few bottles of Cava (usually Martínez) by roughly 40 percent to thicken its texture and concentrate its flavor. The sparkling wine from Spain is known for its crisp minerality and citrus notes, adding a distinct flavor to the foam. Stein combines the Cava reduction with a common custard base — egg yolk, cream, and vanilla — and loads it all into an iSi canister, the tool typically employed in professional bars and kitchens that fluffs up liquids into an airy, soft-peaked consistency. According to Stein, reducing the Cava by nearly half enhances its bitter and acidic elements, giving the otherwise dessert-like custard foam a piquant edge.

“Honesty, I just love crème brûlée and fruit custards in general, so cream and fat is like a match made in heaven with the vibrance and acidity of something like passion fruit,” she says. “As for the sparkling wine, I prefer Cava because I find it to be a little brighter and that it complements the drink’s tropical fruit flavors.”

For the build, Stein brings together a rum base with lime juice and a flurry of passion fruit flavors. The team infuses the rum with a house made bourbon and vanilla bean paste to evoke the profile of a classic Pornstar Martini, typically made with vanilla-flavored vodka and simple syrup. Another key component of a traditional Pornstar Martini is the passion fruit, and here Stein cranks up the passion fruit flavor using passion fruit liqueur, syrup, and pulp. The rum and passion fruit components are quickly shaken with lime juice and poured into a mini-milkshake glass over ice. The lofty spiral of Cava custard foam is the final piece of the puzzle and similarly plays into the Pornstar Martini theme, reimagining the drink’s playful sparkling wine sidecar as an airy foam topping.

Before landing on its current presentation, the drink went through a few iterations. Stein thinks the previous version — where she leaned into her initial crème brûlée idea and caramelized the outer edge of the custard foam with a torch and served the drink in a larger, taller glass — was almost too over-the-top and might have steered customers away. While the drink gained some steam with that presentation, she says it became one of Papi’s best-sellers in its newest get-up.

“Ever since we changed the presentation to a milkshake glass and with two Papi-branded straws, it’s gotten more popular,” she says. “Now, it’s a little cuter, a bit less flashy, a more modest presentation of itself.”

Its visual appeal aside, one of Stein’s favorite aspects of the Mami Chula is its play on competing textures and flavors. With its high fat content, the Cava custard holds its shape and resists mixing into the actual liquid. All the while, the rich and creamy notes of the custard complement the otherwise tart, fruity flavor of the drink. As Stein puts it, the Mami Chula is an “interactive” cocktail: Customers can mix in a certain amount of the velvety foam until the drink reaches their desired level of sweetness.

“It’s a drink that fits both ends of the spectrum,” she says. “I didn’t just want to garnish it with foam for the sake of having a foam. I wanted to create this sort of duality and balance.”

title: The One Food Item You Should Bring Home From Every State [MAP]
summary:
Every state has its own claim to fame — a symbol or tradition that draws in tourists from all over to visit. Louisiana might bring to mind festive Mardi Gras celebrations while New Jersey evokes images of bustling summertime boardwalks. While some are more famed than others, all 50 states have their own specialties that tourists want to experience for themselves. And for many people, bringing home a souvenir for friends, family, or even themselves is non-negotiable. But finding the right souvenir can be a difficult task.

The article The One Food Item You Should Bring Home From Every State [MAP] appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Every state has its own claim to fame — a symbol or tradition that draws in tourists from all over to visit. Louisiana might bring to mind festive Mardi Gras celebrations while New Jersey evokes images of bustling summertime boardwalks. While some are more famed than others, all 50 states have their own specialties that tourists want to experience for themselves. And for many people, bringing home a souvenir for friends, family, or even themselves is non-negotiable.

But finding the right souvenir can be a difficult task. It’s a struggle that often ends in a general store or airport terminal, looking for the least tacky t-shirt to take home. So rather than adding to that magnet or postcard collection, we recommend checking out locally made products that can transport the taste of the region home with you. We previously mapped out the best bourbons, whiskeys, and beers to bring home from each state, but what about specialty food products?

From century-old candy companies and specialty potato chip brands to products that draw from rare local ingredients, read on to discover the most iconic food souvenir to take home from each of the 50 states.

Alabama

Priester’s Pecans

Celebrate a nearly century old Alabama business by taking home a bag of Priester’s Pecans. What later became the official state nut of Alabama, these hand-picked pecans are fresh and full of flavor. The company started back in 1935 when Mr. Lee C. Priester wanted to sell shelled pecans to businessmen at the gas station he owned. One customer requested the pecans to be cracked to take home after his business trip, and this one request led Priester to start Alabama’s largest gourmet handmade candy company.

Alaska

Alaska Kelp Pickles

This Alaskan treat puts a maritime twist on an American fan favorite, using locally harvested bullwhip kelp instead of the typical cucumber. These pickles are a triple threat: they’re packed with vitamins and nutrients, are farmed sustainably, and will surprise you with their salty, savory, and umami-rich flavor profile.

Arizona

Cactus Candy

If using kelp as an ingredient didn’t surprise you, maybe Arizona’s cactus-based candies will. The fruit of the state’s local prickly pear cactus produces a juice or purée used by companies to create a jelly candy similar to a Turkish delight.

Arkansas

Chocolate Gravy

Most people know about the Southern delicacy biscuits and gravy, but Arkansas takes the tradition one step further with chocolate gravy: the sweet, cocoa-flavored counterpart to traditional gravy. While its exact origins remain unknown, the sweet sauce is now a regional favorite in Arkansas and the wider Appalachia area. Chocolate gravy is a game changer for your morning biscuits if you’ve got a big sweet tooth. And you can find mixes easily, like Brenda’s Chocolate Gravy, sold in grocery stores across the state

California

Sourdough Bread

Though you might want to save this errand for the last day of your trip, you can’t leave California without getting some of San Francisco’s famous sourdough. Born in tandem with the California Gold Rush, this style grew to fame when the coastal climate yielded a bread more flavorful and tangier than anywhere else. Now, it’s impossible to leave San Francisco without at least trying its bread, and you might even take home a loaf (or two).

Colorado

Enstrom’s Almond Toffee

Dating back to 1960, Enstrom’s Candy Co. is famed for its almond toffee. The legendary confection is so beloved by locals that it’s commonly referred to as “Colorado crack.” The factory in Grand Junction, Colo. accepts visitors, so guests can see the toffee made up close, and take the chocolate-coated treat home to share afterward.

Connecticut

Munson’s Chocolates

Founded by Ben and Josephine Munson in 1946, Munson’s Chocolates introduced these irresistible, handcrafted confections to Connecticut for the first time. These chocolatiers have built a multi-generational candy family dedicated to making quality chocolate for all — even those in space. In 1995, American astronauts presented a box of Munson’s to Russian cosmonauts aboard the Mir space station. Its chocolates are really out of this world.

Delaware

Fisher’s Popcorn

Rehoboth and Bethany Beach are just two of Delaware’s famous resort towns decked out with boardwalk classics: ice cream, arcades, and most notably, popcorn. Fisher’s Popcorn is a staple for Delaware beachgoers, serving fresh, hand-crafted popcorn that keeps the summer nostalgia going all year round. With plenty of flavors, from Old Bay Dusted Caramel to classic Kettle Corn, Fisher’s makes the perfect souvenir to take home in a tin to your friends and family.

Florida

Key Lime Pie

Named after the Florida Keys, the Key Lime Pie has rocketed to dessert fame over the past century, but its most iconic renditions still come from its birthplace down south. While other states often use the Persian substitute, a real Key Lime Pie is made using its namesake lime variety, making it a must-try even if you’d had the iconic pie before.

Georgia

Georgia Peanuts

Georgia produces more than half of all peanuts in the United States, so it’s no question what you need to bring home from this state. Fresh or honey-roasted peanuts are the go-to snack for travelers since they’re readily available in stores all across Georgia. And if you’re really a big peanut fan, you can visit the World’s Largest Peanut in Ashburn, GA. — a 40-foot-tall monument to the beloved nut — for a great roadside attraction.

Hawaii

Macadamia Nuts

Originally brought to the Big Island as windbreaks for sugar cane fields, macadamia nuts have become one of Hawaii’s most popular specialty snacks. The island climate and volcanic soil provide the perfect environment for the nuts, giving them a creamy, flavorful taste. Mauna Loa sells high-quality, flavored macadamia nuts in most gift shops, or you can purchase from local brands across the islands.

Idaho

Idaho Spuds

No, we’re not suggesting bringing home a bag of potatoes, though that’s not a horrible idea. Idaho Spuds are the cheeky name of a locally beloved potato-shaped chocolate bar. The candy, which comes complete with a gooey marshmallow center and a sprinkling of coconut flakes, has been produced by the Idaho Candy Company since 1918.

Illinois

Garrett Popcorn

Though you might be filling up on deep dish pizza and Chicago-style hot dogs while in town, the Chicago specialty best built to travel home with you is Garrett Popcorn. The family owned shop originally opened in 1949, but the must-try “Chicago Mix” flavor first hit the menu in 1977. Fans would often request an extra bag to combine the shop’s classic CaramelCrisp and CheeseCorn flavors, creating the now-iconic sweet and salty treat.

Indiana

Albanese Gummies

You might recognize this next addition to our list from seeing its gummy bears at your local grocery store, but with more than 500 different kinds of candy, we had to showcase Indiana’s iconic Albanese Candy. The brand makes and sells just about everything at the Albanese Candy Factory Store, where you can see giant chocolate fountains and purchase “goof-ups” at a discounted price. If you’re looking for a gift for a friend with a sweet tooth, Albanese Candy is the perfect place to go.

Iowa

Scotcheroos

Originally a recipe found on the back of Rice Krispies boxes, Scotcheroos are a family gathering classic in Iowa, and for good reason. These no-bake desserts are quick and delicious, made with a base of peanut butter and rice krispies topped with chocolate and butterscotch. Though visitors can typically find these treats at local bakeries, Scotcheroo enthusiasts should head to the Iowa State Fair in August to find some of the best.

Kansas

Sunny Seeds

Every state has its thing, and for Kansas, it’s sunflowers. Sunny Seeds takes the classic salty baseball game snack, and turns it into a chocolate candy-coated treat. You can find these chocolate candies at local retailers and markets across the state.

Kentucky

Bourbon Balls

It’s no surprise that a state famous for its bourbon would make a sweet delicacy out of it too.
Made with pecans, sugar, butter, and Kentucky straight bourbon, you can find this goodie all over the state. Dating back to 1921, Ruth Hunt Candy produces a classic example of the boozy confection, available at its specialty shops around the state.

Louisiana

King Cake

The famous Mardi Gras celebration in New Orleans brings travelers from all over. And if you’re in Louisiana for this iconic holiday, you’ll definitely need to keep a look out for a King Cake — and the baby hiding inside. A nod to the story of the three wise men delivering gifts to baby Jesus, this sweet dough confection hides a plastic baby offering good luck to whoever finds it.

Maine

Whoopie Pie

Although many believe the Whoopie Pie originated from Pennsylvania Dutch bakers, it’s Maine who brought the small cake treat into the spotlight. Initially created with leftover cake batter, whoopie pies were made as an easy, portable treat to take to work. The traditional Whoopie Pie features two small, round cakes with a creamy marshmallow filling. Nowadays, the cake-like treat comes in many flavors, but the first is still the most iconic.

Maryland

Berger Cookies

Known as the “anytime cookie,” Berger Cookies are a staple of Maryland: a soft, cake-like cookie with fudge icing. Henry Berger brought the original recipe to the U.S. in the early 19th century, which was passed down to his descendants and turned into an official brand a century later. While you can find many copycat recipes online, Berger Cookies remains the standard, hand-dipping every cookie it sells.

Massachusetts

Boston Cream Pie

Don’t let the name fool you, the famed Boston Cream Pie is actually a cake. First served at Boston’s Parker House in 1856, French chef Augustine Francois Anezin took the already popular Boston Cream flavor and added it to a dessert. The name came about during a time when pies and cakes were interchangeable, leading to the Boston Creme Pie, and its legacy has lasted the test of time. The original Parker House still sells the iconic pastry, meaning you can visit and see where it all started — and take a few to go.

Michigan

Mackinac Island Fudge

Michigan’s Mackinac Island is famously known as the “fudge capital of the world.” Here, confectioners make around 10,000 pounds of fudge every day, shaping the pieces on large marble slabs — and curious fudge enthusiasts can take in all the action live. Thirteen active fudge-making shops decorate Mackinac Island, making it a popular tourist destination. While you may not be able to bring the show home, you can definitely take back some of the legendary fudge.

Minnesota

Top the Tater Sour Cream Dip

Top the Tater is a legendary dip with deep roots in the Midwest. Though its origins have been lost over time as the recipe was passed from generation to generation, the earliest known mention can be found in an ad for the product in the Winona Daily News in 1962. The dip made with fresh cream from local farms blended with a mix of herbs and spices, has a cult following in the area — Minnesota even throws an annual Top The Tater Days festival.

Mississippi

Mississippi Mud Pie

This delicacy from Mississippi goes by many different names, from “Chocolate Lasagna” to “Mississippi Mud Cake,” but its roots all rest on a gooey foundation of pudding, cake, biscuits, ice cream, whipped cream, marshmallows, and liqueur. Even though it’s named after the (less appetizing) mud that runs along the Mississippi River, this dessert is a delicious Mississippi staple, available at specialty bakeries and gift shops across the state.

Missouri

Red Hot Riplets

With chips specially designed to hold its iconic sweet, hot barbecue seasoning, Red Hot Riplets have amassed a major cult following in Missouri. If you’re willing to take the heat, you’ll have to try this local St. Louis-based brand for yourself, either alone, in a sandwich, or sprinkled on top of a dip.

Montana

Huckleberry Jam

Montana’s high altitude environment provides the perfect habitat for huckleberries, a wild blue-black berry known for its crunchy texture and tart flavor. It’s one of the state’s most popular ingredients, often found in jams, pies, candies, and other treats. If you find yourself in need of a souvenir to preserve the sweet fruit flavor for long after your trip is over, we recommend picking up a few jars of Huckleberry Jam.

Nebraska

Dorothy Lynch Dressing

Although often compared to the widely known French dressing, this small-batch, independent brand makes a dressing unique to the Midwest. Founded in the 1940s, St. Paul-based Dorothy Lynch Dressing, also known to locals as “Dotty,” is a taste of home for Nebraskans. It can go with just about anything: salads, fries, pizzas, marinades, and even cocktails.

Nevada

Ethel M Chocolates

While most things that happen in Vegas might stay in Vegas, sometimes you still want something to remember your trip by. Ethel M Chocolates brings the glamour of Vegas but in the form of glimmering jewel-like chocolates. Founded in 1981, the company rose to fame after Forrest Mars Sr. utilized loose liquor laws in the area to elevate his mother’s traditional recipes, putting liquor in the chocolate to create new, flavorful delicacies. With an annual holiday lights display and premium branding, Ethel M Chocolates stands the test of time for locals and tourists alike.

New Hampshire

Pure Maple Candies

Maple is a well-known staple of northern New England, so it’s no wonder New Hampshire is best known for its melt-in-your-mouth maple candies. These 100 percent pure local maple syrup candies come in all shapes and sizes, giving you plenty of souvenir options to take home to your friends and family.

New Jersey

Salt Water Taffy

While popcorn might be a popular boardwalk snack in other states, arguably the most iconic treat along the Atlantic Ocean is New Jersey’s salt water taffy. It’s a delicious, chewy treat that travels well across state lines, making it the perfect souvenir to take home.

New Mexico

Green Chile Salsa

The green chile is a nostalgic ingredient that runs deep in the culture of New Mexico. The terroir of the high desert environment lends a distinct taste to the local chiles, making them a popular centerpiece for many recipes. Keep an eye out for local salsa bottlings while on your trip, as these can be a great way to package and take home this beloved staple.

New York

Black & White Cookies

While the black and white cookie can now be found in supermarkets across the country, the two-sided snack originally came from New York City, when Bavarian immigrants John and Justine Glaser opened Glaser’s Bake Shop in 1902. The cookie stood out with its cake-like base and even split of chocolate and vanilla icings. While the original Glaser shop closed in 2018, there are still countless other spots to snag a standout black and white cookie: William Greenburg, Barney Greengreass, and Orwashers — just to name a few.

North Carolina

Moravian Cookies

Originally a type of German ginger cake, Moravian cookies came to central North Carolina in the 18th century and were adapted into the now-famous paper-thin crisp wafer. And as of 2026, it was formally designated as the official state cookie. Only a few other states have an official treat, including one on our list (Maine’s Whoopie Pie). A class of fourth graders were the ones who vouched for the Moravian cookie, and now we’re vouching for it too.

North Dakota

Chocolate-Covered Potato Chips

Famously known as “chippers,” chocolate-covered potato chips are a hidden gem of North Dakota. It’s surprising that this snack isn’t more popular around the country, given America’s track record with chocolate-covered treats, but it just makes this North Dakota delicacy even more special. Widman’s Candy popularized this combo in the mid-20th century when it began selling hand-dipped chippers made with locally sourced Red River Valley potato chips. You can now find versions of the original treat at candy stores and gift shops around the state.

Ohio

Buckeyes

Inspired by the official name of Ohio, “the Buckeye State,” these peanut butter candies mimic the appearance of both the Buckeye tree and the eyes of a buck deer. Buckeyes are no-bake confections made by mixing powdered sugar, peanut butter, butter, vanilla and salt. This combination is rolled into small balls and dipped three-fourths of the way in melted chocolate. You can find them in local bakeries all across Ohio.

Oklahoma

Smoked Bologna

Though barbecue is everywhere in the south, Oklahoma rarely gets the spotlight. But the Sooner State does have one specialty that it can claim as its own: Smoked bologna.The regional delicacy first rose to popularity in the mid-20th century as a cheaper alternative to other smoked meats, but more recently it’s become a point of regional pride. Oklahoma delis source local meat for you, making it a step up from your usual lunch meat.

Oregon

Pear Hazelnut Fruit Pâté

You can find hazelnuts and pears in abundance across Oregon: The state produces 99 percent of the country’s hazelnuts, and pears act as its official state fruit. This product from Oregon Growers allows visitors to take home two local delicacies in one. Its fruit pâtés, including the Pear Hazelnut, are sweet jams made in collaboration with local farmers, created to be served alongside your favorite cheeses.

Pennsylvania

Tastykakes

All Pennsylvanians remember opening their lunchboxes as a kid to find a Tastykake iced loaf cake waiting inside. This iconic snack cake brand has been a phenomenon in the Philadelphia area for over a century. When Philip J. Baur and Herbert T. Morris started the Tastykake brand in 1914, the treats were originally delivered in horse-drawn wagons. Now, Tastykake products have made their way onto shelves all around the Northeast, featuring a wide range of treats from frosted and cream-filled cupcakes to chocolatey, peanut butter sponge cakes. But the fresh-baked iced loaf cakes will remain a cornerstone of Pennsylvania nostalgia forever.

Rhode Island

Pizza Strips

Most people are familiar with the classic New York slice, Chicago deep dish, or even Detroit-style pizza, but did you know Rhode Island has its own iconic pizza serve? Known as party pizza or pizza strips, this style offers up thick slices of focaccia-like crust, covered in tomato sauce, and served at room temperature. While pizza doesn’t normally travel well, this Rhode Island delicacy can be packaged and taken across state borders without losing its quality.

South Carolina

Benne Wafers

A Charleston staple since the mid-20th century, Benne Wafers are a cookie that combines locally grown sesame seeds with butter, brown sugar, flour, and vanilla. It gets its name from benne, the original name of the sesame plant, brought over from Africa. The crisp wafer is treated as a symbol of good fortune, sent home with visiting guests to wish them well. Its intricate history and subtle flavor make it the perfect souvenir to take home with you.

South Dakota

Dakota Style Chips

Potato chips are an American staple, but South Dakota has its own spin on the classic. Dakota Style is a brand founded in 1985 by Bob and Betty Campbell, making potato chips with bold flavors and old school packaging that highlights its humble roots. These chips are known for their extra-thick cut, making for an industrial strength crunch. Visitors can find these in grocery stores across the state, or they can purchase directly from the Dakota Style Foods official store in Clark, S.D.

Tennessee

Goo Goo Clusters

Right in the heart of Tennessee, Nashville paved the path for the candy industry with America’s first combination candy bar, Goo Goo Clusters. The product features layers of roasted peanuts, marshmallow nougat, and caramel, all coated with delicious milk chocolate. While it never rocketed to Hershey-level fame, Goo Goo Clusters are where the combination candy started.

Texas

Texas BBQ Sauce

Barbecue is a hot topic when it comes to Texas. The start of the barbecue sauce craze goes back to 1934, when a group of Syrian and Lebanese immigrants hosted barbecue fundraising dinners, and among these events came the rise of the 1934 barbecue sauce. Texas BBQ sauce tends to be more tangy and savory, built to honor the flavor of the meat. When you’re passing through grocery stores or local shops, turn to brands like Stubb’s Original Legendary Bar-B-Q Sauce or the 1934 BBQ Sauce, or seek out the beloved Goldee’s BBQ Sauce, available at the famed restaurant and select retailers.

Utah

Chocolate-Covered Cinnamon Bears

America loves to cover everything in chocolate, and it doesn’t stop in Utah, either. The Sweet Candy Company took this trend to the next level in 1994 by covering its red, gummy cinnamon-flavored bears in chocolate. Now, this unusual combination of flavors is sold across the state in grocery stores, specialty shops, and even college campuses.

Vermont

Maple Syrup

While Vermont maple syrup — known for its impeccable quality and pure, fresh taste — is a grocery store staple across the country, it’s still worth seeking out the specialty during your next visit. Visiting or buying syrup from local producers like Little Hogback Farm in Bristol and Couching Lion Maple Sugar Farm in Huntington will bring you even close to the source.

Virginia

Peanuts

While Virginia doesn’t produce nearly as many peanuts as Georgia, Virginia peanuts, also known as “gourmet” peanuts, have the largest kernels and are more celebrated for snacking, especially in-shell at ballparks. Specialty stores like The Peanut Shop in Williamsburg or Whitley’s Peanut Factory in Glen Allen will give you direct access to the state’s famous gourmet peanuts.

Washington

Aplets & Cotlets

Inspired by the iconic Turkish Delight, Aplets & Cotlets are a Washington-born jelly candy made in the early 1900s by Armenian immigrants Armen Tertsagian and Mark Balaban. The two founders took advantage of Washington’s healthy apple and apricot economy, combining the fresh taste of the fruits with the delightful crunch of walnuts. These local delicacies are usually found at gift shops all around the state.

West Virginia

Pepperoni Roll

What started as a quick, shelf-stable snack for coal miners has turned into this state’s most iconic combination food, the Pepperoni Roll. Bakers stuff a fresh roll of pizza dough with pepperoni sticks or slices to make a snack similar to a calzone. Its original home, the Country Club Bakery, still prepares fresh, pepperoni-stuffed rolls by the hour.

Wisconsin

Wisconsin Cheese Masters

No state is as serious about their cheese as Wisconsin; it holds five out of seven of the “Best Cheese in America” titles in recent years. European immigrants propelled Wisconsin into cheesemaking glory by bringing over traditional techniques that outclassed other states. Now, there are a handful of specialized retailers that will serve you the state’s award-winning cheeses: Wisconsin Cheese Mart, in both Milwaukee and Madison; Wisconsin Cheese Masters, hidden up north in Door County; Cheese Brothers, settled in the city of Barron — along with tons of smaller, local creameries.

Wyoming

Buffalo and Elk Jerky

Beef jerky is a popular roadside snack, but guests making a stop in Wyoming, can find niche variants like buffalo and elk jerky. You’ll have to travel to one of the state’s speciality stores to find the local delicacy, but the increased flavor and nutrients will make it worth the trip. Luckily, there are plenty of butcher shops along all of the state’s highways, so you’ll just have to keep an eye out as you go.

content:
Family ties have long been integral to the tequila industry. Some of the world’s greatest agave spirits come as a result of multiple generations passing down the traditions and techniques of tequila making. Many brands receive that savoir-faire from just one family — but for Don Fulano, the knowledge of two long-standing tequila families informs the process.

Co-founders Enrique Fonseca and Sergio Mendoza founded Don Fulano in 2002. Sergio is a fourth-generation agave farmer, distiller, and blender, and Enrique is a fifth-generation agave. Together, their wealth of knowledge and commitment to artisanal practices established one of the most celebrated modern tequila brands.

Today on the “VinePair Podcast,” Sergio joins Adam to discuss his family’s long history in the tequila business, how he and Enrique launched their brand, and what it’s been like living through the tequila boom.
